topicName: Thread Dumps and Heap Dumps Analysis (JVM Performance)
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Thread Dumps and Heap Dumps Analysis (JVM Performance)"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Analyzing Java Virtual Machine (JVM) performance under load is a critical skill for performance testers. When performance degradation, high CPU usage, or OutOfMemoryErrors occur, thread dumps and heap dumps provide the definitive diagnostic data needed to find the root cause."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding Thread Dumps"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"A thread dump is a snapshot of all active threads running in the JVM at a specific moment in time. It shows the call stack for each thread, revealing what methods are being executed, thread states (RUNNABLE, WAITING, BLOCKED), and potential deadlocks."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"RUNNABLE: The thread is executing in the JVM or waiting for CPU resources."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"BLOCKED: The thread is waiting to acquire a monitor lock to enter a synchronized block."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"WAITING / TIMED_WAITING: The thread is waiting indefinitely or for a specified time for another thread to perform a specific action."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"How to Capture a Thread Dump"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"During a performance test, you can capture thread dumps using built-in JDK command-line utilities. Taking multiple thread dumps spaced 5 to 10 seconds apart helps identify whether a thread is genuinely stuck or progressing slowly."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"jstack -l <pid> > thread_dump.txt"},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding Heap Dumps"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"A heap dump is a binary snapshot (typically in .hprof format) of all objects currently residing in the JVM memory heap. It includes object sizes, references, and class hierarchies. Heap dumps are essential for diagnosing memory leaks, high garbage collection overhead, and OutOfMemoryError exceptions."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"How to Capture a Heap Dump"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can manually capture a heap dump using the jcmd or jmap utility. Alternatively, you can configure your application to automatically generate a heap dump when an OutOfMemoryError occurs by using JVM flags."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /path/to/heap_dump.hprof"},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/path/to/dumps/"},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Analyzing the Data"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"Manual analysis of large thread and heap dumps is impractical. Performance engineers use specialized graphical analysis tools to interpret these files efficiently."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Thread Dump Analyzers: FastThread, IBM Thread and Monitor Dump Analyzer (TMDA), and VisualVM."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Heap Dump Analyzers: Eclipse Memory Analyzer Tool (MAT), VisualVM, and YourKit."},{"order":21,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices in Performance Testing"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"Always monitor resource utilization (CPU, memory, GC activity) alongside your load generator. When performance degrades, orchestrate thread dumps immediately to capture bottlenecks, and reserve heap dumps for analyzing memory retention profiles after test completion."}]
